sites.name: Hogsback Camp, Heliotrope Ridge
sites.capacity: Numerous flat gravel and snow platforms along the moraine crest; the busiest camp on the north side and it fills on summer weekends
sites.water: Melt streams run below the moraine and near the trail crossings through most of the climbing season, but they retreat with the snowpack and can be gone or badly silted by late August — carry a stove capable of melting snow late in the year
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit; camping is dispersed and unregulated apart from wilderness rules (12-person party limit, no campfires at this elevation). A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
sites.notes: The default first night for parties on the Coleman-Deming and the usual staging point for the North Ridge, on the moraine bench above the trail's stream crossings about 2.5 to 3 miles in. Access is the current problem rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road, the only driving approach, was damaged in the December 2025 floods and has been under a repair closure short of the trailhead, which turns the approach into a long road walk or bike ride — confirm the road status with the ranger district before committing to a weight-carrying plan. Waste handling has varied year to year, with toilets present some seasons and pack-it-out blue bags the rule in others, so carry bags regardless. Snow usually covers the camp until well into June, which makes a flat platform easier to find and liquid water harder.

sites.name: Kulshan Cabin site and Harrison Camp
sites.capacity: Several small forested and moraine-edge sites; more sheltered and lower-capacity than the Hogsback
sites.water: Reliable — the approach streams below the moraine still carry water here later in the season than they do higher up, though the crossings themselves can run high and pushy on warm afternoons
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit required; Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge.
sites.notes: The cabin itself is long gone, and the name now marks a cluster of sites around 4,800 to 5,000 ft with Harrison Camp on the moraine above the lower Coleman. These suit a party arriving late, anyone who wants trees around them in bad weather, or a group that would rather climb from lower down than share the Hogsback. The trade-off is an extra thousand feet on summit day. Backcountry toilets have been maintained here in some seasons but not others, so plan to pack waste out.

sites.name: Upper Coleman Glacier snow camps, below the Black Buttes
sites.capacity: Whatever platforms your party digs; commonly used between roughly 7,000 and 7,200 ft, with room for a handful of tents but no established sites
sites.water: None you can rely on — this is a melt-snow camp, so budget fuel accordingly. Occasional surface runoff appears on the rock of the Black Buttes in hot spells but should not be planned around.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit for camping. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
sites.notes: Pushing camp onto the glacier below the Black Buttes cuts a real chunk out of summit day and puts you above most of the weather that sits on the moraine. It costs you a fully exposed camp on snow, so platforms need walls, and everything about the site depends on that year's crevasse pattern — what was a flat bench one August can be broken up the next. Parties are already roped and on glacier travel terrain to reach it, which rules it out for anyone wanting a simple carry. Wind is the usual reason people retreat from here to the Hogsback.

sites.name: Colfax-Grant saddle bivy
sites.capacity: One or two small parties at most; an exposed high point rather than a campsite
sites.water: None. Melt snow, or carry everything from lower on the route.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
sites.notes: The saddle between Colfax Peak and the main summit is occasionally used as a very high bivy by strong parties shortening summit day, and more often as an emergency stop by parties caught out by weather or a slow descent. It is fully exposed to wind and to whatever the mountain is doing, with no shelter of any kind, and the Roman Wall above it is not somewhere to be improvising in a storm. Treat it as a contingency rather than a plan unless the forecast is settled and your party is fast. It is also the last place on the route with any option other than continuing up or going down.

sites.name: Sandy Camp, top of the Railroad Grade
sites.capacity: The main climbers' camp on the south side, in a sheltered sandy basin at the crest of the moraine; multiple tent sites, busy in July and August
sites.water: Contested and season-dependent. Some parties find runoff at the north end of the camp and on the rocky ground above it; others arrive to find nothing exposed at all and must melt snow. Plan for melting and treat running water as a bonus.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest — the approach runs through the Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and the upper moraine into Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit. A recreation pass is required to park at the Schriebers Meadow / Park Butte trailhead. Registering your climb at a ranger station is voluntary but sensible.
sites.notes: The standard Easton Glacier high camp, reached by following the Railroad Grade moraine up from Schriebers Meadow and Morovitz Meadow. The basin gives real wind protection, which is why it is preferred over the more scenic but more exposed ground on the moraine crest itself. The gravel road in is snowbound into June in most years and is rough enough to be worth checking before a long drive. There have been seasons with no toilet facilities anywhere on the mountain, with blue bags issued free at the Sedro-Woolley ranger office, so carry a pack-out system.

sites.name: Railroad Grade and Morovitz Meadow camps
sites.capacity: Scattered sites in the trees behind the eastern moraine and on the ridge east of the Railroad Grade, roughly 5,500 to 5,800 ft; smaller and quieter than Sandy Camp
sites.water: Generally reliable — meadow streams and melt channels run here later into the season than they do at the top of the moraine, which is much of the reason to camp low
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (Mt. Baker National Recreation Area and Mount Baker Wilderness). No overnight permit; recreation pass required to park at Schriebers Meadow.
sites.notes: These lower sites suit parties arriving in the evening, anyone wanting shelter from wind, and low-snow years when the higher ground has no water at all. They are meadow and subalpine terrain, so camp on durable surfaces and off the vegetation, which is slow to recover here. Summit day from this elevation is long, and most parties treat these as a first night before moving camp up rather than as a base for the climb. In heavy snow years the alternative runs the other way and people camp as high as 6,800 ft because that is where flat snow is.

sites.name: North Ridge glacier bivy, upper Coleman
sites.capacity: Dug snow platforms for one or two parties; no established site, and the usable spot moves year to year
sites.water: None reliable. Melt snow, and carry enough fuel for a party that will also be melting for the climb.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No permit required to camp. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead.
sites.notes: North Ridge parties generally carry from the Hogsback out onto the Coleman and bivy somewhere around 6,800 to 7,000 ft to shorten the approach to the base of the ridge, which itself rises around 4,000 ft to the summit. Where exactly that camp sits is decided by crevasse conditions on the day rather than by any fixed location, so it is worth arriving with daylight left to scout. The camp is on glacier, exposed, and above the point where you can retreat without roping up. The same Glacier Creek Road closure that affects the Coleman-Deming applies to this whole approach, so confirm road access first.
